Matsya Avatar

Matsya Avatar

The world saved in the flood — in everyday English

Vishnu's first avatar, and the story of King Manu

How to read this book

This book is meant to be read together, sitting side by side, out loud. The story is in simple, everyday English, but its ideas are big — grown-ups will find plenty to think about, and young listeners will be able to picture every scene.

Yellow boxes — in them, the characters speak in their own voices. Read them slowly, with feeling.

(Words in purple are cues for the reader — don't say them out loud, do them. Like pausing here for a moment, or lowering your voice.)

Big words are for sounds — rain, waves, thunder. Say them loudly, with gusto.

Green boxes — Pause and think — they come at the end of every part. Stop there, listen to the questions, and let the listener speak first. Finding the right answer is not the point; talking about it is.

The main source of the story is the Bhagavata Purana (Book 8, Chapter 24) . Where other tellings differ a little, that is noted separately at the end — nothing has been mixed into the middle of the story.

Meet the characters

King Manu (Satyavrata) — a king who left his kingdom behind and was doing tapasya (spiritual discipline) on a riverbank. Kind, calm, and true to his word. By the end of this story he becomes Vaivasvata Manu — the father of the human beings of the new age.

The little fish — Matsya — first a tiny fish that could fit in the palm of a hand, then bigger than the sea itself. In truth, this is Lord Vishnu himself — Vishnu of the blue radiance, golden crown and yellow robes, who took the form of a fish to save the world. This is considered Vishnu's first avatar .

The Saptarishi — the seven great sages. Keepers of knowledge and tapasya. In the flood they sit in the boat, so that knowledge is not wiped from the world.

Vasuki the serpent king — the great serpent king. In the flood he becomes the rope that ties the boat to the fish's horn.

Hayagriva — the demon with a horse's head. While Brahma slept, he stole the Vedas from beside him and hid deep in the sea.

One thing to remember — in this story the smallest creature speaks first, and the greatest work begins with protecting her.

Part 1
The little fish's cry for help

A very long time ago. King Satyavrata — whom everyone called Manu — had left his kingdom behind and was doing tapasya on a riverbank. Every morning he would step into the river, fill his cupped hands with water, and offer arghya — water offered in worship — to the sun.

One morning, just as he had filled his cupped hands with water, something fluttered.

Splash-splash… splash!

In his cupped hands was a tiny golden fish — smaller than a finger. Manu was about to tip her back into the river when the fish spoke. (Here, make your voice very soft and small)

The little fish: Save me! The big fish in the pond will eat me! Don't put me back in the river!

Manu stopped short. So tiny a fish — and so afraid.

A tiny life in the palm of a hand

Manu put the fish into his kamandalu (water pot) and took her back to his hermitage.

Manu: Don't be afraid. I will protect you.

Here is an old idea worth understanding — matsya-nyaya, the law of the fishes. It is the rule of the watery world: the big fish eats the little fish, and the little one has no one to listen to her. That is what happens when the strong crush the weak and no one stands in between.

That day, Manu stood in between. A king's true work is not picking up a sword — it is protecting the one who cannot protect herself.

The fish grew calm in the kamandalu. Manu smiled. Little did he know — this promise of his was going to turn out far, far bigger than he imagined.

Pause and think — If a very small and frightened creature asked you for help, what would you do? And think about this — Manu gave his promise without stopping to think. Do we ever know, before we make a promise, just how big it will grow?

Part 2
From the water pot to the sea

The next morning Manu came to the kamandalu — and stopped. In a single night the fish had grown so big she could not even turn around inside it.

The fish: King, it is very cramped here. Give me a bigger home.

Manu put her into a large earthen pot . But by evening even the pot was too small. Then a tank, then a pond — every home too small within a few days!

The kamandalu grew too small — so, the pot.

The pot grew too small — so, the tank.

The tank grew too small — so, the pond.

The pond grew too small — so, a great lake.

The fish kept growing even in the lake — as big as an elephant, then bigger still. The villagers would gather on the bank and just stare. Manu took her to the river Ganga . But before long, even the river began to feel cramped for the enormous fish.

The fish: King, now only one home is left for me — the sea. Take me to the sea.

With the help of hundreds of people, and with great difficulty, Manu brought the fish to the seashore.

The moment she slid into the waves of the sea, the fish grew even more enormous — mountain-sized. Her golden body shone in the sunlight, and a strange peace spread over the water.

Manu stood on the shore, hands folded, watching. One thought was growing clearer and clearer in his mind — this is no ordinary fish. How could a creature that goes from the palm of a hand to the sea in a week possibly be ordinary?

Pause and think — Each time, without tiring, Manu found a bigger home for the fish. He never once said — enough, no more. Why do you think that was? Can helping someone sometimes be tiring too?

Part 3
The truth, and the warning

Manu asked, hands folded —

Manu: Who are you? You are no ordinary fish. Tell me the truth.

At that moment a blue-and-golden light spread over the waters of the sea. The fish's voice was now deep and calm — as if it echoed through the whole sea.

Matsya: Manu, I am Vishnu. I have taken the form of a fish to save the world. Your kindness has pleased me — you saved the small one, so in a great crisis I stand with you.

Then the voice grew grave. (Here, make your voice slow and deep)

Matsya: Listen carefully. On exactly the seventh day from today a great deluge will come. The rain will not stop, the rivers will overflow, the sea will swallow the earth. The whole world will drown in water.

Manu's heart began to race. But Vishnu also showed him the way —

Matsya: Build a very strong, large boat . Seat the Saptarishi in it. Keep the seeds of every plant, and pairs of every living creature, with you. When the waters come, don't panic — I will come.

Manu did not waste a moment. Craftsmen gathered. Tap-tap, knock-knock — day and night, the boat took shape. Baskets of seeds were filled, herbs were bundled, pairs of creatures were gathered.

Seven days — that was very little time. But Manu did not lose time to panic. He shared out every job: someone to bring wood, someone to look after the seeds, someone to call the sages.

By the sixth day the boat was ready — tall, strong, and holding everything from which the world could begin again: knowledge (the sages), seeds (the plants), and life (the pairs of creatures).

On the morning of the seventh day, everyone's eyes turned to the sky. Clouds were gathering. There was a strange smell in the air — the smell of a coming storm.

Pause and think — Vishnu gave Manu seven days — no more, no less. If you learned that everything would change in seven days, what would you save first? Manu did not save gold and silver — he saved seeds, creatures and knowledge. Why?

Part 4
The flood of the deluge

On the seventh day, first the clouds thundered —

Rumble… crash!

Then the rain began. Rain like no one had ever seen.

Patter-patter-patter-patter…

The rivers overflowed. Ponds, lakes — all became one. Water poured into the villages, fields drowned, and only the branches of trees could be seen. The sea, forgetting its bounds, climbed onto the land. Whichever way you looked, there was only water.

Manu, the Saptarishi, the seeds and all the creatures were in the boat. The boat rocked on the waves — now up, now down. All around was darkness, noise and fear.

Then, far off, among the waves, a golden light gleamed. (Here, bring hope into your voice)

Manu: Look! He has come!

A drowned world, a tiny boat

The boat tied to the horn

The great Matsya came up to the boat. On his head was a great horn . Manu took Vasuki the serpent as a rope and tied the boat to that horn — the knot pulled tight, with trust.

Then began that strange journey — nothing but water, and a calm, strong fish pulling the boat. Matsya was in no hurry. Like a great, experienced sailor — straight, slow, unafraid.

On the long journey, Matsya kept telling Manu words of wisdom — what the mind is, what the soul (atman) is, how to stay calm in fear, and how the world is made again even after it is unmade. The sages listened in silence. These are the very teachings that later became the root of a whole Purana.

Pause and think — All around, only water, darkness and noise — yet the people in the boat were calm. Why? Perhaps because they trusted that someone who knew the way was pulling them. How much does trust help in difficult times?

Part 5
The stolen Vedas

It was not only lives that were caught in the flood — another precious thing was in danger: knowledge.

This happened very long ago. Brahma, tired, had fallen asleep. At that moment the demon with a horse's head, Hayagriva , crept in and carried off the four Vedas kept beside him. The Vedas — that is, all the gathered knowledge of the world: farming, medicine, songs, hymns, ways of living.

Hayagriva: If knowledge stays with me, the world will live in darkness — and in darkness, the rule will be mine!

Hayagriva took the Vedas and hid in the deepest, darkest bottom of the sea. He thought — who will find me at such a depth?

But he had forgotten — the sea is Matsya's own home.

Matsya dived into the depths. In the darkness his golden radiance spread like a sun. Hayagriva tried to fight, but how long can darkness stand before light?

One flash of light… and that was all!

(Don't stretch the battle out here — pause for a moment, then go on in a calm voice) In a single glimpse, the battle was over. Hayagriva met his end, and the Vedas were back with Matsya — safe, whole and complete.

Just think — in the flood, Vishnu saved two things: life and knowledge. In the boat were seeds and creatures, and from the bottom of the sea the Vedas returned.

Because merely living is not enough. If knowledge were wiped away, the new world would have to learn everything from nothing again — how fire burns, when seed is sown, which herb works in sickness.

Matsya returned the Vedas to Brahma. As if the last copy in a library had been rescued from a fire and put back on its shelf.

Pause and think — If all the world's books and all its knowledge vanished one day, what loss would hurt the most? And think about this too — Manu saved seeds, Matsya saved knowledge. Without which of the two could the world still carry on?

Part 6
The waters went down

Then one morning, the rain stopped. The clouds cleared. The roar of the waves slowly faded — and the boat came to rest on a high place. It was a peak of the Himalayas. (Here, make your voice completely calm and gentle)

Manu and the Saptarishi stepped out of the boat. Below, far and wide, the water was going down and the wet earth was breathing again.

Now the real work began. Manu sowed the saved seeds in the wet soil. The pairs of creatures were set free in the open. The sages began to share knowledge again. Slowly, the world grew green, full and alive once more.

Matsya came to take his leave. As he went, he said —

Matsya: Manu, remember — what you save in the flood decides what kind of world will be made. You saved life, you saved seeds, you saved knowledge — so this world will be good again.

This very Manu came to be called Vaivasvata Manu — the father of the human beings of the new age. And that tiny fish, who one day trembled in the palm of a hand, is remembered forever as Vishnu's first avatar — Matsya .

Pause and think — The story began with a little fish and ended with a new world. What was the link in between? A promise given by a king — and kept right to the end.

In the end — a little more thinking

Beginning with protecting the small. Saving the world did not begin with a war. It began with saving a fish trembling in a palmful of water. The one who hears the cry of the small and helpless is the one fit for great work.

A promise that kept growing. Manu's promise began with a kamandalu and reached the sea. Each time the work was bigger than before — and each time Manu did not step back. A good promise is one that is kept even when it gets hard.

Seeds and knowledge — that is how a world is saved. Manu did not save a palace; he did not save treasure. He saved seeds, creatures and sages; Matsya saved the Vedas. Whatever can grow onward — that is the future.

Questions for the listeners:

1. If the fish had gone to someone else instead of Manu — someone who would have laughed and tipped her into the river — how would the story have gone?

2. In your own 'boat', which three things would you definitely keep — and why?

3. Where do we see matsya-nyaya, the law of the fishes, in today's world? Who could stand there as 'Manu'?

Sources and other tellings

Main source: This story is told chiefly according to the Bhagavata Purana, Book 8, Chapter 24 — Satyavrata (Manu)'s tapasya, the growing fish, the seven days' warning, the boat with the Saptarishi and the seeds, the boat tied by Vasuki to the horn, and Manu becoming Vaivasvata Manu at the end — this sequence comes from there.

Other tellings (footnotes):

1. The Mahabharata (Vana Parva) tells this story as narrated by the sage Markandeya. There the fish warns Manu of the flood at the end of Brahma's day, and the peak where the boat comes to rest is called 'Naubandhana' — the peak where the boat was tied, or came to rest.

2. The Matsya Purana says that the wisdom Matsya gave Manu on the long flood journey later became the root of a whole Purana — that is, the story's greatest gift is considered to be its teaching.

3. Hayagriva and the Vedas: The stealing of the Vedas from Brahma by Hayagriva and their return by Matsya is placed by some tellings before the flood and by some in that same period; the time-order differs, the event does not. In this book it is kept in a separate part alongside the main Bhagavata story, in the form in which it is traditionally told together with it.

4. In some tellings the flood is called the deluge at the end of a kalpa (an age of the world), and the list of creatures Manu saved is given in more detail. The main point is the same in all — protection, the boat, and a new beginning.

All the pictures in this book were newly made for this story — in the traditional ink-line and flat-colour style. No picture has been cropped.
